claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential should be trained by active learning on a strategically limited set of high-fidelity ab initio calculations.
The training calculations explicitly retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The ML potential can serve as a surrogate for ab initio interactions.
ML interatomic potentials can attain near-DFT energy accuracy in a multicomponent refractory alloy.
Active learning will identify key ab initio data points and capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling with minimal computational overhead.
Nested interpolation or a comparable accelerated integration scheme will efficiently bridge the free-energy differences between solid and liquid phases.
Combining the ML potential with accelerated free-energy integration will preserve chemical accuracy for phase free energies.
The proposed workflow will provide high-fidelity fusion properties for both solid and liquid phases in elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems.
Fusion free energies can be reproduced with mean energy deviations of only a few meV per atom.
Melting temperatures and fusion-related entropy measures will be reproduced within chemical accuracy.
The proposed workflow will be 10–100 times faster than full ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows.
The proposed workflow will scale better to multicomponent high-entropy alloys than TOR-TILD.
The method should match established elemental and binary benchmarks and extend reliably to multicomponent alloys.
The intended composition domain extends from pure elements and binaries to high-entropy alloys.
The intended temperature domain extends from just below melting through unspecified high-temperature regimes.
The ML model may fail to fully capture electron–vibration coupling in complex multicomponent systems.
Active-learning performance may be unreliable when extrapolating beyond densely sampled training regions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that active learning captures electron–vibration coupling, while the uncertainty field concedes that the model's ability to capture that coupling in complex multicomponent systems is unresolved.
The predicted outcome says the method will extend reliably to multicomponent alloys, whereas the uncertainty field questions robustness when extrapolating to sparsely sampled regions.
